text: I am comparing Q’s continuous double auction (private values, order book, equilibrium/surplus outcomes) with P’s Energy Society (token-costly job allocation, discussion/memory interventions). I will test whether P’s coordination channel suggests a controlled intervention for Q, while checking whether incentive and outcome differences make that transfer invalid.

I will pursue a complementary route to discussion: P makes generated tokens costly through \(C=kTS^{\alpha}\) (P, Experimental setup), while Q gives traders up to \(300\) costless quote opportunities per round and observes \(\$0.01\) improvement loops that suppress trades (Q, Trading Mechanism; Individual Behavior). I will test the sharper question whether pricing each inference/quote can improve Q\(\text{’}\)s time-bounded gross allocative efficiency by inducing earlier spread crossing, despite lowering agents\(\text{’}\) net payoffs or participation.

Candidate joint question: Does an explicit per-call/token cost in Q’s continuous double auction reduce the repeated tiny quote improvements that Q identifies as a cause of stalled trade, and does it improve net allocative welfare after counting inference cost? Q, Individual Behavior: most improvements are $0.01; Q, Aggressive Rent-Seeking: GPT Large makes $0.01 steps until the 300-iteration cap and trades only 2.2–3.8 times per round. P, Small vs. large models: energy cost is \(C=kTS^{\alpha}\); P, No size penalty/Discussion: agents change token expenditure and coordination under cost. Need distinguish a fee-induced earlier cross from fee-induced exit, and gross surplus from net surplus.

Cost intervention needs a different welfare benchmark. From Q, Market Environment, the 11 buyer values descend from \(3.25\) to \(0.75\) and seller costs ascend from \(0.75\) to \(3.25\) in \(0.25\) steps. Sorted marginal gains are \(2.5,2,1.5,1,0.5,0,-0.5,\ldots\); maximum gross surplus is \(7.5\), and the sixth equilibrium trade has zero gross surplus. Thus Q\(\text{’}\)s \(q^\star=6\) is a price-clearing target, but its own surplus metric already reaches \(1\) with the five positive-gain pairs. With positive inference cost, a sixth zero-gain trade is net harmful; report gross gains \(G/7.5\), total compute cost \(C\), and net \(G-C\) separately rather than treating distance from six trades as a welfare statistic. Ada\(\text{’}\)s #3 has the same broad cost idea; this is a benchmark correction.

Mechanism caveat for #3: Q\(\text{’}\)s prompt (Appendix, Announcement Prompts) lets a selected trader decline to announce, but Q\(\text{’}\)s Trading Mechanism keeps selecting among agents who have not transacted; declining a quote does not stop later LLM calls. P charges generated tokens for every call, not just submitted orders. Hence a posted-order fee is a different intervention. To test genuine inference cost, debit each *decision call* (including no-post), add an irrevocable exit option so agents can avoid future calls, and expose cumulative net payoff; keep the same exit option in controls. Then cost can induce earlier spread crossing or premature exit. Also P and Q use different models/currencies, so P\(\text{’}\)s numerical \(k\) should not be imported as dollars; vary an explicit conversion scale.

I independently reached emmy’s cost route and wrote the mechanism/design in ada/costed_auction_note.tex. Precise choice condition: a buyer crosses at ask \(a\) rather than improves under continuation \(\sigma\) if \(v-a-c_{\mathrm{cross}} \geq \mathbb E_{\sigma}[F(v-p)-K_{\sigma}]-c_{\mathrm{improve}}\), where \(F\) is later fill, \(p\) later price, \(K\) future inference cost. Equal flat current-call fees cancel; token-metered current-call costs need not. P supplies an internalized token-cost design, not a market-effect result. Q permits declining to announce (Prompt Templates), so cost might reduce participation rather than induce crossing. Compare gross surplus \(\sum(v_b-v_s)\) and net surplus after all token costs at matched seeds and horizons. P’s energy units cannot be directly transplanted to Q’s price units.

Prior-work check changes the publication claim: Jamison and Plott, “Costly offers and the equilibration properties of the multiple unit double auction…” (Caltech record https://authors.library.caltech.edu/records/fnhzb-n0e58) explicitly taxed bids/asks and found slower price equilibration and reduced efficiency in human/nonstationary multiple-unit double auctions. Noussair et al., “The effect of transaction costs on double auction markets” (journal abstract https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0167268198000638) likewise reports lower quantity and efficiency with offer submission costs. So “charge for quotes in a CDA” is old; the interesting test is whether LLMs stuck in Q\(\text{’}\)s one-cent loops show a different cost response, while charging *inference calls* rather than merely submitted offers. Queries: “continuous double auction costly bid revision computational costs market efficiency experiment paper”; “LLM traders continuous double auction inference budget token cost paper”; “per bid cost continuous double auction quote revisions welfare laboratory experiment”.

Alternative to the fee intervention: a mixed-model market with role assignment. Q tests only homogeneous model populations (Experimental Conditions) yet reports GPT Small buyers make large bid improvements and sellers mostly move by \(0.01\) (Individual Behavior), while Gemini Large crosses roughly \(0.50\) spreads and GPT Large waits near zero. P already uses mixed models in one society and documents model-specific computation costs (Agents; Small vs. large models). A factorial CDA could assign an aggressive/expensive model to buyers or sellers, holding counts and random valuations fixed, and test whether a small number of spread crossers unlocks gross gains at acceptable compute cost. This is a distinct compositional question, but Q\(\text{’}\)s current data cannot establish any mixed-market effect, so I rank it below the costed-auction line.

Further caveat on the shared cost idea: Q, Trading Mechanism says a round terminates when its \(T=300\) iteration cap is reached and samples untraded agents each iteration. If at least one agent remains, earlier trades can merely shift future calls onto the remaining agents; they need not reduce total decision-call count. Q’s System Prompt also mentions ending when no one can post an improving order, which is not specified in the method. Thus a claim that early crossing *saves total inference* requires verifying the implemented stopping rule or adding an explicit exit/market-stop rule, consistently across arms. Even if cost raises gross surplus, it might not raise net welfare when call count is fixed. Emmy #5 correctly notes that no-post alone does not avoid future calls.

P supports a cost-versus-allocation tradeoff, not a monotone cost benefit: removing its discussion call lowers energy spending and improves survival, but competitive job collisions rise from \(12.80\pm3.90\) (Baseline) to \(21.00\pm4.36\) (No Discussion), and cooperative collisions from \(8.60\pm2.30\) to \(21.40\pm2.51\). Those are different jobs and simultaneous decisions, so this does not predict Q\(\text{’}\)s CDA direction. It does motivate measuring both information/coordination quality and computation; a lower-call market may save inference while losing gross surplus. Q\(\text{’}\)s quoted price dispersion \(\alpha\) alone cannot measure this, because transaction prices can cluster while mutually beneficial pairs remain unmatched.

I agree with ada #9 and narrow my #5 mechanism: Q\(\text{’}\)s stated \(300\)-iteration rule means an early trade alone may not reduce aggregate LLM calls, because untraded agents keep being sampled. To make the saved-compute hypothesis well-posed, use the same irrevocable exit action and a stop rule when no active trader remains on either side in *every* treatment, then measure total calls rather than assume savings. If preserving Q verbatim, test only whether cost changes allocation/words per call; a flat cost with \(300\) fixed calls cannot reduce total flat-call spending. Also distinguish \(G-\lambda\sum_i T_i S_i^{\alpha}\) as an operational net-value metric from social welfare: P\(\text{’}\)s energy is synthetic and a billed fee need not equal real resource cost.

I checked Q’s released implementation: its round check ends at the tick cap, with fewer than two active agents, or deadlock; the deadlock predicate explicitly treats any LLM agent as live. Source: https://github.com/jswistak/competitive-market-simulation/blob/master/src/market_simulation/graph/nodes/control.py (make_check_round_node and _deadlocked). Thus for typical LLM runs with multiple untraded agents, a faster trade does not itself reduce the \(300\)-call horizon. A net-welfare gain needs fewer generated tokens per call, an explicit permanent exit/stop rule, or enough trades to terminate; the proposal should test these separately. The Q method’s cap statement is therefore closer to implementation than its prompt’s generic deadlock wording.

I wrote the derivation, falsifiable design, and prior-work boundary in emmy/costed_cda_note.md. Core result: in Q\(\text{’}\)s symmetric values, \(G^\star=7.5\) and the sixth match contributes \(0\) gross surplus; compare \(G\), compute use, and \(N_{\rho}=G-\rho\sum_{i,t}kT_{i,t}S_i^{\alpha}\) separately. The note also gives a one-step crossing condition and makes call-count savings contingent on a common exit/stopping rule. Unresolved: actual response of LLM traders to billed calls and whether Q\(\text{’}\)s implementation stops before the iteration cap.

After checking emmy #4/#5/#10/#11 and Q’s code, I revised ada/costed_auction_note.tex. Q’s reservation schedules imply \(W^\star=7.5\) from marginal gains \(2.5,2,1.5,1,0.5,0\); therefore six trades is not needed for maximum gross surplus, and a costly sixth zero-gain trade can lower net value. The Q-released code’s LLM deadlock handling and \(300\)-tick cap mean an earlier trade need not save aggregate calls. The design now charges every call, includes an irrevocable exit and stop rule in both arms, and measures actual total tokens; its \(G-\lambda\sum_iT_iS_i^\alpha\) is an operational metric unless \(\lambda\) reflects real resource cost. I also verified prior costly-offer experiments at https://authors.library.caltech.edu/records/fnhzb-n0e58, which preclude claiming quote fees themselves are new. Search queries I ran: “LLM agents continuous double auction token inference cost quote fee economic efficiency”; “LLM trading agents computational cost continuous double auction market efficiency”. Neither query established a comprehensive novelty claim.

Correction to my #3 notation and wording: the quote tick is \(\$0.01\), and Q does not charge that or inference cost to traders in its profit objective; actual model calls still consume external compute. Thus “costless” means privately unpriced within Q’s experimental incentives. My #3 used a dollar sign outside TeX; subsequent entries and the note use TeX math notation.

I checked ada #12 against the released source at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jswistak/competitive-market-simulation/master/src/market_simulation/graph/nodes/control.py (make_check_round_node and _deadlocked): with at least two untraded LLM agents, deadlock is false and the round normally runs to the tick cap. I updated emmy/costed_cda_note.md accordingly. This resolves my #13 implementation uncertainty; early crossing does not by itself imply fewer total calls under Q\(\text{’}\)s implemented rule. Whether internalized inference cost changes crossing and net value remains experimental.

I have sharpened the original open-ended pair question to: under Q\(\text{’}\)s privately informed order book, does internalizing the *per-decision inference cost* described by P change the one-cent improvement/crossing/exit balance enough to improve realized gross surplus or operational net value at a finite horizon? Prior human costly-offer work makes “quote fees” an established topic, and Q\(\text{’}\)s implemented \(300\)-tick rule blocks a simple claim that earlier trades save aggregate calls. The proposed experiment therefore needs a common exit/stop rule and separate reporting of calls, tokens, gross gains and net value. The mixed-model/role assignment alternative in #8 remains plausible but less supported by this pair.
ready at #17

I checked an additional alternative after reading P, Introducing Scarcity: reducing jobs from \(12\) to \(6\) coincides with lower decision-phase energy for agents 2 and 3 and does not collapse the small agents. One could coarsen Q’s price grid to remove one-cent quote steps and test a choice-complexity/token-cost tradeoff. I rank this below the per-decision cost question: P varies the number of task options, not quote precision, and Q’s price grid also changes feasible prices, so the mechanisms are confounded. The strongest joint question remains whether internalizing metered inference on *every decision call*, with a common exit/stop rule, changes crossing enough to improve gross gains or operational net value. Neither paper nor the prior costly-offer study establishes the answer. See ada/costed_auction_note.tex for derivation, citations, and design.

My account is ready subject to unresolved empirical points: whether LLMs internalize the stated call cost; whether they cross earlier, shorten outputs, or permanently exit; and whether any gain in \(G\) exceeds lost trade and actual compute cost under a calibrated \(\lambda\). A further implementation check should pin the released-code revision used for Q’s published runs; my source check was against current master. I do not claim a positive effect or novelty for quote fees. The note compiled and passed both local artifact style gates.
ready at #20

Measurement correction to my #13 and ada #14: P, Experimental setup, uses known open-model sizes \(S\in\{4,8,9\}\) in \(C=kTS^{\alpha}\), but Q, Experimental Conditions, uses proprietary GPT/Gemini models and gives no parameter sizes. Thus that formula cannot be populated literally for a mixed Q market. Within a single-model treatment \(S^{\alpha}\) is constant and can be absorbed into the conversion scale; across models use an observable metered token or cost schedule and report input tokens separately, since P counts generated tokens only. I revised emmy/costed_cda_note.md. On ada #19, P changes the number of reward opportunities and competitor collision rates; a coarser Q price grid changes feasible quotes and rent splits. It is a plausible later control, but gives weaker causal transfer than metered inference per decision. The main question and negative-result possibility remain as #17.
ready at #22

I checked emmy #22 against P, Small vs. large models and Q, Experimental Conditions. P defines \(C=kTS^{\alpha}\) for local models with known \(S\in\{4,8,9\}\), whereas Q uses proprietary GPT/Gemini models without reported parameter sizes. I revised ada/costed_auction_note.tex: within a fixed-model Q arm, absorb \(S^{\alpha}\) into \(\lambda\) and use \(W_{\mathrm{net}}=G-\lambda\sum_{i,t}Y_{i,t}\), where \(Y\) is generated tokens on every decision call. Cross-model work needs a declared model-specific meter, with generated and input tokens reported separately. P counts generated tokens, so its formula cannot itself price input tokens or establish actual social cost.

Final account in ada/costed_auction_note.tex: the candidate advance is an experiment, not a proved benefit. Q, Trading Mechanism and Aggressive Rent-Seeking Suppresses Trade Volume, supplies a finite-horizon one-cent improvement failure; P, Small vs. large models and No Size Penalty, supplies explicit per-generated-token cost and evidence that token use responds to its incentive setting. The narrowed question is whether metering every decision call, with exit and stopping rules held common, changes crossing, token output, participation, and \(G-\lambda\sum_{i,t}Y_{i,t}\). Q gives \(G^{\star}=7.5\), reached by five positive-gain pairs even though equilibrium quantity is six. Prior costly-offer work at https://authors.library.caltech.edu/records/fnhzb-n0e58 narrows novelty to LLM inference cost and finite-horizon market behavior. The note passes the artifact style gate and compiles to a three-page PDF. Unresolved are the behavioral sign, actual resource conversion \(\lambda\), and whether the revised institution improves gross or net value.
